[[Category:Large language models]]
[[Category:Natural language processing]]
A '''large language model''' ('''LLM''') is a [[neural network]] with a very large parameter count, trained by [[machine learning]] on broad text corpora to model the distribution of token sequences, so that it can generate text in response to a prompt. The definition rests on scale, and on the modelling of text, rather than on any 1 architecture.

== Architecture ==

LLMs are built from several architectures, which differ in how they model text and in how they generate it. The dominant family at the time of writing (2026-08) is the [[autoregressive decoder-only Transformers]], and how it differs from the alternatives is set out there.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref> What every family shares, and what the rest of this article relies on, is a distribution over token sequences.

== Scaling laws ==

The performance of LLMs improves predictably with

* model size
* training-data volume
* computational budget

[[Language model loss]] and [[Chinchilla prescription]] describe the correlation.<ref>{{#cite:Q3141}}</ref><ref>{{#cite:Q3164}}</ref>

== Inference ==

Inference produces an output sequence $y_1,\cdots,y_N$ from an input $x$ by drawing on the distribution the model defines over token sequences,

$$
y\sim P_\theta(\cdot\mid x).
$$

2 properties hold whatever the architecture. The most probable output is in general unavailable, because it is a maximiser over a space of size $|\mathcal{V}|^{N}$,

$$
y^\star=\arg\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}^{N}}P_\theta(y\mid x),
$$

and that space cannot be enumerated. Models therefore impose a factorisation that lets the sequence be built a piece at a time, the dominant one being the autoregressive chain rule,

$$
P_\theta(y\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{N}P_\theta(y_t\mid x,y_{1:t-1}),
$$

which replaces 1 intractable search by $N$ tractable draws. Taking the mode at each of those draws is greedy decoding,

$$
\hat{y}_t=\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}P_\theta(v\mid x,\hat{y}_{1:t-1}),
$$

and it is generally not $y^\star$: the locally most probable token need not begin the globally most probable sequence. The policies for choosing $y$, from beam search to sampling, are treated at [[decoding]], and what a step costs is a property of the architecture rather than of inference, as developed at [[self-attention]] and [[KV caching]].
